extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, PTO examiners, and litigants (patent attorneys and judges)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for evaluating when prosecution laches bars issuance or enforcement of a U.S. patent (including in § 145 actions), focusing on unreasonable delay, prejudice, totality of circumstances, and exemplary reasonable/unreasonable conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of prosecution laches in § 145 actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO may assert the prosecution laches defense in a § 145 action brought by a patentee to obtain a patent; it would make little sense to allow the PTO to deny issuance on laches grounds but not to defend against issuance in a § 145 action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTO can assert prosecution laches even if it did not previously issue rejections or warnings regarding prosecution laches during prosecution. New evidence and arguments are admissible in § 145 proceedings (Kappos v. Hyatt; Troy v. Samson), so the PTO may raise meritorious defenses in that forum. The fact the PTO did not previously warn the applicant may be considered in the totality of circumstances but does not bar assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of prosecution laches defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution laches requires proving two elements: (a) the patentee’s delay in prosecution was unreasonable and inexcusable under the totality of the circumstances, and (b) the accused infringer suffered prejudice attributable to the delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish prejudice, an accused infringer must show evidence of intervening rights — that the accused infringer or others "invested in, worked on, or used the claimed technology during the period of delay." (Cancer Research). Both elements must be considered under a totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality of the circumstances inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: "An examination of the totality of the circumstances, including the prosecution history of all of a series of related patents and overall delay in issuing claims, may trigger laches."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis is not limited to the prosecution history of the particular application at issue; courts should consider a series of related applications (e.g., continuations, families) and overall patterns of delay. Focusing narrowly on only the specific applications can be error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreasonable and unexplained delay — magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether delay is unreasonable depends on the specific circumstances; historically, the Supreme Court found delays of eight to nine years sufficient to render patents unenforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past cases (Woodbridge, Webster Electric, Bogese) found eight- to nine-year delays enough; in this case, delays of 12–28 years (or even 7–19 years under later priority dates) were held sufficient. Magnitude of delay is a key factor but must be considered with other circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice requires intervening rights/investment
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish prejudice, the accused infringer must show evidence of intervening rights — that the accused or others "invested in, worked on, or used the claimed technology during the period of delay."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of intervening rights or business investments/use during the delay period is necessary; mere passage of time without such prejudice may not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO delay is relevant but cannot excuse applicant delay
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO’s delay in prosecution may be considered in the totality of circumstances, but the PTO’s delay "cannot excuse the appellant’s own delay."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTO delays are a weak reason to negate prosecution laches (patent term adjustment provisions already address PTO delay). Courts should not shift primary blame to the PTO where applicant conduct caused unreasonable delay. The PTO’s procedural choices (e.g., compact prosecution) do not, by themselves, absolve applicant conduct that produces prejudice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable examples of delay (non-exhaustive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of reasonable delay include: (i) filing a divisional application in response to a restriction requirement, even if filed immediately before issuance of the parent; (ii) refiling an application to present new evidence of an invention’s unexpected advantages; and (iii) refiling to add subject matter to support broader claims as development progresses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These examples are not exhaustive; an applicant could reasonably refile where the refiling "is not unduly successive or repetitive." Courts should consider the context and purpose of refilings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of unreasonable delay / egregious misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Unreasonable delays involve repetitive refilings that demonstrate unjustifiable prosecution delay, for example, "refiling an application solely containing previously-allowed claims for the business purpose of delaying their issuance." Repeated continuations without amendment or addressing rejections (Bogese) and other conduct that "deliberately postponed meaningful prosecution" are examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing multiple continuations without meaningful prosecution, adding claims solely to delay issuance, or other patterns that 'deliberately and consistently' produce exceptional delay can warrant laches. Filing claims previously lost in interference is an example of patently unreasonable conduct (even if purposeful state of mind is immaterial).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution conduct characteristics that indicate undue delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain prosecution features can make examination effectively impossible and support a laches finding: claiming many priority dates, long/complex specifications, extremely large claim counts across applications, repeatedly adding hundreds of claims that restart examination, filing identical or patentably indistinct claims across different applications, and rewriting claims mid-prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These combined characteristics create a 'perfect storm' that overwhelms examiners' ability to determine priority, perform double-patenting analyses, or identify written description support. Evidence that prosecution "all but guaranteed indefinite prosecution delay" supports unreasonable delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden-shifting once PTO presents laches evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient prosecution laches evidence and argument presented by the PTO at trial can shift the burden to the applicant to justify the prosecution conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court held that the PTO’s prosecution laches evidence in this case was enough to shift the burden to Hyatt; once PTO establishes a prima facie case under the totality, the applicant must provide reasonable explanations for the delay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant’s equitable obligation beyond statutes/regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant must prosecute its applications in an equitable way that avoids unreasonable, unexplained delay that prejudices others; compliance with statutes and PTO regulations alone does not guarantee immunity from prosecution laches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecution laches places an additional, equitable restriction on patent prosecution conduct beyond statutory/regulatory obligations. Applicants cannot simply rely on formal compliance if their overall conduct abuses the patent system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal notice not strictly required for laches
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution laches does not strictly require formalized notice, warnings, or office actions, although those may lend support to a prosecution laches finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While formalized PTO warnings or rejections may strengthen a laches case, courts may find laches based on the totality of the record and pattern of conduct even in the absence of explicit prior PTO laches rejections.
